title: World Bank Raises India's FY27 Growth Forecast to 7.1%, Flags AI as Next Driver
excerpt: The multilateral lender lifted its 2026/27 estimate by 50 basis points on resilient domestic demand, while warning that oil prices, El Niño and market volatility threaten the outlook.
body:
• The World Bank raised India's GDP growth forecast for 2026/27 to 7.1%, up 50 basis points from its June estimate, citing resilient domestic demand, government measures that shielded consumers, and strong remittances — and lifted South Asia's 2026 growth outlook by 60 basis points to 6.9%.
  • Risks are stacking up: persistently high oil prices from supply disruptions linked to the US-Israeli war on Iran, a possible strong El Niño that could dent farm output and rural demand, and a global market correction that could trigger capital-flow volatility. Inflation is expected to stay elevated into 2027.
  • Artificial intelligence is the report's big upside bet: 23% of Indian firms now report using AI, against 43% of US firms, and the Bank says wider adoption could lift productivity, create more and better jobs, and raise India's potential growth.
  • For readers with money ties to India: the RBI is widely expected to raise its benchmark rate by 25 basis points on October 7 — its first hike since 2023 — which could push up loan costs for borrowers in India while giving NRIs slightly better yields on NRE and NRO fixed deposits.

The World Bank on Tuesday raised its forecast for India's economic growth in 2026/27 to 7.1%, a 50-basis-point upgrade from the 6.6% it projected in June, — an upgrade published in the Bank's latest India Development Update that rests on resilient consumption, government steps to insulate households from high fuel prices, and steady remittance inflows.

India's 7.1% forecast still trails the 8.6% growth recorded in 2025/26, and the report cautions that momentum may fade in the second half of the current fiscal year.

Consumption holds up while prices stay high

The Bank also raised its growth forecast for the whole South Asia region to 6.9% for 2026. World Bank Chief Asia Economist Franziska Ohnsorge told Reuters the resilience was striking: "higher energy prices have not interrupted momentum in consumption growth," she said, crediting "government measures to shield consumers, strong remittances and resilient domestic demand" for cushioning the impact of supply disruptions linked to the US-Israeli war on Iran.

That strength has come with an uncomfortable side effect: higher inflation has been eroding consumers' purchasing power even as growth held steady — a decoupling Ohnsorge described as "quite striking." Inflation is expected to remain elevated into 2027, and the Bank warned that in emerging markets, the normal lag between such shocks and their effect on output is around 18 months.

India's central bank expects inflation to average 5% in the current financial year, according to Reuters, and a majority of economists polled by the news agency expect the Reserve Bank of India to raise interest rates by 25 basis points on October 7 — its first increase since 2023 — with another hike likely in December.

AI takes center stage as the upside story

The report gives artificial intelligence special focus, arguing India is unusually well placed to harness it thanks to a large technical workforce, a globally integrated IT services sector, and its digital public infrastructure. Some 23% of Indian firms report using AI, compared with 43% of American firms — a gap the Bank reads as headroom for rapid catch-up.

"One promising avenue for creating more, better jobs is the widespread deployment of AI. AI adoption in South Asia remains well behind that in advanced economies, but is catching up fast."

— World Bank, India Development Update

Global Capability Centres — the offshore hubs of multinational firms that increasingly anchor India's services exports — employed 1.9 million professionals in 2024, rising to 2.36 million in 2025, the report noted. The Bank urged South Asian governments to adopt AI to sustain growth momentum over the medium term.

What it means for the diaspora

For Indians abroad, the near-term variable that matters most is the RBI's expected October 7 rate decision. A first hike since 2023 would feed through to deposit rates — good news for NRIs holding NRE or NRO fixed deposits — while borrowers in India would face higher EMIs. Persistent inflation also erodes remittance value: rupees sent home buy less when consumer prices run hot.

The Bank also cites strong remittance inflows as one of the reasons domestic consumption held up — a direct endorsement that puts the diaspora inside the growth story, not just observing it.

What's next

Three things to watch: the RBI's October 7 decision and whether a second hike follows in December; crude prices, which remain the single biggest swing factor for India's import bill while the US-Israeli conflict disrupts supply routes; and the weather — a strong El Niño could squeeze monsoon rainfall, rural demand and food inflation, biting directly into the domestic-consumption engine the forecast depends on.

If the risks stay contained and the AI productivity story accelerates, 7.1% could prove conservative. The Bank's own warning stands: with an 18-month lag between price shocks and their growth impact, the bill for today's inflation may not yet have arrived.
